title: Power Peaks at a Middle Load

scenes.tts: A muscle lifts nothing. It shortens as fast as it can, and it does no external work. Another muscle holds a load it cannot move. It also does no external work. At both extremes, the external work is zero. So where does a muscle deliver its power? In 1938, A V Hill asked what sets how fast an activated muscle shortens.

scenes.visual: Two labelled muscle blocks, one with no load shortening fast, one holding a heavy block that does not move; both labelled external work zero; a question mark between them.
scenes.narration: A muscle lifts nothing. It shortens as fast as it can, and it does no external work. Another muscle holds a load it cannot move. It also does no external work. At both extremes, the external work is zero. So where does a muscle deliver its power? In 1938, A. V. Hill asked what sets how fast an activated muscle shortens.

scenes.tts: Hill used isolated frog sartorius muscles at about 0 degrees Celsius. He tetanized each muscle. Then he let it shorten against a series of loads on a lever. A thermopile recorded the heat. He read the speed from the record of shortening, not from the total distance shortened. Heavier loads gave slower shortening.
scenes.visual: Muscle block pulling a lever with a light, a medium and a heavy load in turn; speed arrow shrinks as load grows; a thermopile block labelled heat. Caption marks the picture schematic.
scenes.narration: Hill used isolated frog sartorius muscles at about 0 degrees Celsius. He tetanized each muscle. Then he let it shorten against a series of loads on a lever. A thermopile recorded the heat. He read the speed from the record of shortening, not from the total distance shortened. Heavier loads gave slower shortening.

scenes.tts: Speed fell with load along a curve called a rectangular hyperbola, not along a straight line. A viscous brake would give a straight line. So Hill's result ruled out a passive viscous-elastic muscle. Here is the curve for a made-up model muscle, not measured human values. Its isometric force is 100 newtons. With no load, it shortens at 0.40 metres per second. At 100 newtons, it does not shorten.
scenes.visual: Speed against load plot: a dashed straight line for a viscous brake, then the hyperbola drawn under a made-up-model heading shown from the start from Hill's equation for the model muscle, endpoints labelled.

With no load, it shortens at 0.40 metres per second. At 100 newtons, it does not shorten.

scenes.tts: Power is force times speed, in watts. With no load, the speed is greatest, but the load is zero, so the power is zero. When the load equals the force the muscle can hold, the speed is zero, so the power is zero again. This is external power, not A T P use. An isometric muscle does no external work, yet it keeps splitting A T P.

scenes.tts: In between, power peaks. In this model, the constant a is one quarter of the isometric force. Then the peak sits near 0.31 of the isometric force. That is a load of 30.9 newtons. The speed there is about 0.12 metres per second, and the peak power is about 3.8 watts. The exact fraction depends on the curvature.
scenes.visual: Dot stops at the power peak; guide lines drop to the load axis and across to the speed curve; values labelled.

scenes.tts: Now stretch the same model fibre. Assume force falls along a straight line, from full force at 2.2 micrometres of sarcomere length to zero at 3.65 micrometres. At 3.00 micrometres, the isometric force is 44.83 newtons. The peak power falls by the same factor, 0.448. The speed at peak power stays at 0.309 of top speed. Hill's rule gives no molecular mechanism, and its constants are frog values at about 0 degrees Celsius. External power is zero at both extremes and peaks at a middle load.
